ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Companies Act 1993 (Public Act 1993 No 105, as amended), Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (Public Act 2009 No 35), AML/CFT (Definitions) Regulations 2011, and Companies Office UBO disclosure rules administered by the Registrar of Companies. For any China WFOE in the ultimate ownership chain, PBOC/SAMR Order No. 3 (effective 1 November 2024) requires Government_Only_Access UBO disclosure.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Incorporation of each ultimate beneficial owner (parent entity)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Registrar of Companies or other competent corporate registry in the country of origin
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: If the origin country is a Hague Apostille Convention state: notarize (if required), apostille by the origin competent authority, then deliver to the New Zealand Companies Office. If the origin country is not an Apostille member: notarize, then consular legalization by the New Zealand Embassy/Consulate or other recognized consular post; the two authentication routes are parallel and mutually exclusive and are never chained.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Good Standing / Certificate of Compliance of the immediate parent entity
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Corporate registry or authorized commercial register in the parent entity's domicile
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille route for Apostille member states: issue original, obtain apostille, submit to New Zealand Companies Office. Non-member states: issue original, notarize, obtain consular legalization from the New Zealand consular post in the issuing state; apostille and consular legalization are parallel and mutually exclusive and must not be combined sequentially.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Board Resolution / Power of Attorney authorizing incorporation of NZ Ltd and appointing initial directors and shareholders
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Board of directors of the parent/ultimate beneficial owner entity
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Certified true copy signed by the corporate secretary; notarize before a notary public; if the jurisdiction is an Apostille member, apply for a Hague Apostille through the local competent authority; if not, obtain consular legalization through the destination country's consular representation in the issuing jurisdiction; never use apostille and consular legalization sequentially.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Articles of Association / Constitution (certified copy) for each corporate UBO
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Parent/UBO company or its registered agent in the country of origin
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Certified by the registered agent/company secretary; then either Hague Apostille by the competent authority of the origin state (Apostille member) or consular legalization by the New Zealand Embassy/Consulate in the origin state (non-member); the routes are alternatives, not cumulative.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Bank Reference Letter for each significant UBO or parent entity
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Qualifying bank maintaining the UBO's/parent's verified account
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Original letter on bank letterhead, issued within 90 days; if the bank's country is an Apostille member, the bank's signature/seal must be apostilled by the local competent authority; if not, the bank document is notarized and then consular-legalized by the relevant consular authority; apostille and consular legalization are parallel and mutually exclusive.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certified passport and residential proof for each UBO, director, and authorized signatory
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Notary public or equivalent public officer in the individual's country of residence
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Notarized identity and proof of address; for Hague member states, apply for apostille from the domestic competent authority; for non-members, use consular legalization through the relevant embassy/consulate; no sequential combination of apostille and consular legalization is permitted.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: All directors, shareholders, named officers, ultimate beneficial owners, authorized signatories, and material counterparties must be screened before incorporation against the UN Security Council Consolidated Sanctions List, OFAC SDN and Non-SDN lists, the UK HMT Consolidated Sanctions List, EU consolidated sanctions, and New Zealand sanctions measures administered by MFAT under the Russia Sanctions Act 2022 and the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009. Domestic and foreign politically exposed persons (PEPs) and their family members and close associates require enhanced due diligence, identification of source of wealth and funds, senior-management approval, and continuous transaction monitoring. Any positive hit, unresolved name match, or anonymous/opaque nominee relationship must be escalated to the AML compliance officer before name clearance, and a suspicious transaction report must be made to the NZ Financial Intelligence Unit where required.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office - Name Availability Check and Reservation (Companies Register system, companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Company names are registered in Latin characters; Maori macrons and diacritical marks are accepted where available. Non-Latin scripts such as Chinese characters are not permitted as the statutory company name; an English phonetic transliteration or a secondary trade name may be used. The four-tier naming convention is: Tier 1 available name, Tier 2 reservation, Tier 3 near-identical name requiring consent, and Tier 4 prohibited or sensitive name requiring prior ministerial approval.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If the Registrar rejects a proposed name, the applicant may request written reasons and submit an application for reconsideration with a corrected name, the applicable regulator's written consent for any sensitive token, and evidence that the name is not identical or almost identical to an existing registered name. incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (NZ), as amended, including the incorporation and registration provisions (ss 10-15), company name and registered office provisions (ss 20-24), directors and officer appointments (ss 31-39 and ss 151-158), share subscription, consideration and capital provisions (ss 49-63), share registers and records (ss 86-113), and directors duties and board resolution provisions (ss 122-149 and ss 159-190); together with the Companies Regulations 1994 and, where a public securities offer were ever made, the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 (not applicable to the present private subscription).
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), Wellington, New Zealand
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Application for Registration of a Company (online form NZCN/01) filed through the Companies Office electronic register at www.companiesoffice.govt.nz
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: None: New Zealand imposes no minimum paid-up or subscribed capital and no blocked escrow account for an ordinary limited liability company. The company may be incorporated with nil paid-up capital. Shares can be issued for any lawful consideration, including cash, property, services, or future promises, provided the board complies with the consideration and allotment rules in Companies Act 1993, ss 49-58 and the solvency test where distributions or redemptions are involved. All allotments must be entered in the share register within 10 business days.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en:
RESOLUTIONS OF THE FIRST MEETING OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF [COMPANY NAME] LIMITED (COMPANY NUMBER [NUMBER])

A meeting of the board of directors of the Company was duly convened and held on [date] at [time] at [registered office address], or by electronic communication, under the Companies Act 1993 and the Constitution of the Company. The following directors were present: [Director A] (Chairperson), [Director B], and [Director C]. The Chairperson confirmed that notice of the meeting had been given in accordance with the Constitution and that a quorum existed.

RESOLVED as follows:

1. Constitution and registered office. The draft constitution tabled at this meeting is adopted as the Company’s constitution, effective on the date of registration. The registered office of the Company is fixed at [full street address, city, New Zealand], and that office shall be accessible during ordinary business hours and used for all statutory communications. The directors are authorized to complete and file all necessary forms with the Registrar of Companies for the registration of the Company, the constitution, the registered office address, the address for service, and any electronic addresses for service.

2. Subscription, allotment and share capital. The share subscription schedule submitted to this meeting is approved, including for each subscriber the class, number, nominal value, issue price and amount paid or unpaid on each share. The directors are authorized and directed to allot shares to the persons so listed, to enter the allotments in the share register, to issue share certificates or electronic entitlements, and to take all steps required by ss 49-58 of the Companies Act 1993, including any solvency confirmation where required.

3. Appointment of statutory officers. [Director A] is appointed Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, [Director B] is appointed Company Secretary, and [Director C] is appointed Chief Financial Officer, each with the authority and duties determined by the board. Each officer is authorized, subject to board supervision, to sign and deliver documents, to make statutory declarations and filings with the Companies Office and Inland Revenue, and to appoint professional advisers, auditors, legal counsel and agents on behalf of the Company.

4. Banking and payment operations. The opening of transaction accounts with [bank name], including New Zealand dollar, United States dollar and, where available, digital asset or USDC settlement accounts, is approved. The Chairperson, Managing Director and Chief Financial Officer are jointly and severally authorized to execute account documents, set payment limits, sign cheques, authorize electronic funds transfers, instruct foreign exchange, and manage card and API settlement arrangements with payment processors such as Stripe, provided that all transactions are recorded and reported within the board’s delegation matrix.

5. General authorization and ratification. All pre-registration agreements, applications and acts of the subscribers done in the Company’s name are ratified. Any director or officer may execute all agreements and instruments necessary to open bank accounts, lease premises, subscribe for cloud data-center services, and procure intellectual property insurance. Certified copies of this resolution shall be furnished to banks, payment processors and regulators as conclusive evidence of the authority conferred.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Pre-incorporation name search and corporate eligibility verification
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, online Companies Register at www.companiesoffice.govt.nz, accessed by RealMe login or public search.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Perform an online name-search on the Companies Register using the exact proposed name and any phonetic equivalents. Verify that the name does not include a prohibited expression, imply governmental connection, or conflict with an existing registered company or trademark. If the name is available, prepare to submit it with the incorporation application because New Zealand does not require a separate name-reservation fee. Confirm nationality and residence requirements for directors under section 151(2) of the Companies Act 1993: at least one director must live in New Zealand or be an eligible Australian resident director. Where a foreign corporate shareholder or director executes documents outside New Zealand, arrange notarization, apostille or certified English translation of the execution pages before incorporation; New Zealand local signers generally do not require notarization.
required_dossiers: Applicant and director passport or national identity card (certified if issued outside New Zealand)
Proof of residential address for every director and shareholder
Address for service in New Zealand (physical street address, not a PO Box alone)
Certificate of incorporation and good standing for any corporate shareholder or corporate director
Notarized power of attorney or certified English translation of foreign documents, if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is rejected, use the Companies Office refusal reason and refile with a changed distinctive element. An applicant may also apply for consent to use a restricted name under ss 22-24 of the Companies Act 1993; alternatively, proceed under a new available name.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Preparation of constitution, statutory consents and anti-money-laundering dossier
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Companies Office; overseas notarial authorities for foreign execution; registered office service provider if used.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Draft the constitution in accordance with the Companies Act 1993 if the subscribers do not intend to rely solely on the statutory default regime. The constitution should specify share classes, transfer restrictions, director appointment and quorum thresholds, and permissible indemnity and record-access arrangements. Prepare and execute a share subscription and allotment schedule, and complete the Companies Office Consent to Act as Director for each director. Collect proof of identity, residential address, citizenship and tax identification numbers for every beneficial owner and controller, and obtain a registered-office acceptance letter from the service provider or landlord. Where documents are signed overseas, have the execution pages notarized and apostilled by a competent notary in the jurisdiction of execution; no separate notarial filing is otherwise required for the New Zealand Companies Office.
required_dossiers: Proposed company constitution, or a written resolution adopting the default statutory constitution
Full legal name, date and place of birth, nationality, residential address and tax number of each director
Consent to Act as Director forms
Share subscription and allotment schedule with subscriber names, class, number of shares and consideration
Registered office consent and address for service letter
AML/CFT customer identity, beneficial ownership and source-of-funds evidence
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Companies Office notifies a defect in the consents or constitution, cure the issue by filing a fresh Consent to Act or by statutory declaration under section 34 of the Act. If rejection is due to unreadable foreign documents, resubmit certified English translations within the response period stated in the notice.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Electronic filing and payment of the registration application to the Registrar
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office online portal via RealMe business login.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Log in to the New Zealand Companies Office online registration application and follow the Register a Company workflow. Enter the approved company name, intended shareholders and director details, proposed share capital including zero-paid or unpaid capital if any, registered office and address for service in New Zealand, and the initial accounting preference. Upload any custom constitution and signed Consent to Act forms, answer the compliance and solvency declarations truthfully, and nominate electronic filing details. Pay the registration fee, currently approximately NZD 105.40 including GST, using a credit or debit card. Review the final application summary, submit the application, and retain the transaction reference. The Registrar will issue the electronic Certificate of Incorporation and allocate a New Zealand Company Number, generally within one to two working days after successful validation.
required_dossiers: Completed online incorporation application, equivalent to Form NZCN/01
Signed constitution and director consents uploaded or linked
Payment confirmation for the official filing fee
Final registered office and service-address data
Directors statutory declarations and solvency confirmation
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried or suspended, the Registrar will issue a notice specifying the defect. Correct the application through the pending-application dashboard as soon as practicable. If the defect is not corrected within 20 working days, the application is treated as withdrawn and the applicant must re-submit and pay a new filing fee. Use the Companies Office online support channel to expedite review after correction.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Post-registration statutory activation: tax, banking, share register and annual return calendar
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office; Inland Revenue (IRD and GST); approved New Zealand bank or payment institution; WorkSafe New Zealand only if employing staff.
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Immediately after receiving the Certificate of Incorporation, hold the first board meeting and minute the resolutions covering registered office, banking, statutory officers, share allotment and delegation. The appointed officers must register the company with Inland Revenue to obtain an IRD number, register for GST if taxable supplies reasonably exceed NZD 60,000 within 12 months, and register as an employer for PAYE if employees will be hired. Open bank or electronic-money accounts with a New Zealand bank or approved payment partner by providing the certificate, director registers, share register and beneficial ownership declarations, and complete know-your-business and source-of-funds checks. For non-resident operations, assess transfer pricing and any United States tax information requirements if US-source payments are collected. File annual returns with the Companies Office on or before the incorporation anniversary, and notify any registered office, director, or share allotment changes online as they occur.
required_dossiers: Certificate of incorporation and current Companies Office company extract
First board resolution and officer appointment minutes
Share register, share certificates and subscriber allotment documentation
IRD number application and GST/PAYE registration details
Bank account opening pack, KYB documents, Stripe agreement and USDC settlement provider contracts
Compliance calendar for annual return, income tax return and GST return
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a post-registration filing is late or rejected, submit a voluntary disclosure to Inland Revenue and apply for penalty remission under the Tax Administration Act 1994. If the annual return is overdue, file it immediately and pay the late fee; a formal notice of proposed removal from the register can be cured by filing the overdue annual return and any outstanding confirmation before the stated deregistration date.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not Applicable. No industrial licensing board, municipal industrial permitting authority or manufacturing inspectorate is engaged because the entity is a pure digital cloud-based generative AI, LLM inference and API token provider under ISIC 6201.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Not Applicable. New Zealand does not issue an operating license for ISIC 6201 software, AI or API services. The only statutory obligations relevant to digital operations are privacy, tax and consumer-law compliance, not industrial licensing.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Not Applicable. The Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) New Zealand and territorial authorities acting under the Resource Management Act 1991 have no jurisdiction over a software/AI API service with no physical production footprint.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt. The activity is not a prescribed or permitted industrial activity under the Resource Management Act 1991, and no Environmental Impact Assessment, notice of requirement or resource consent is required for cloud-code development, API hosting or consulting services.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not Applicable. There are no point-source wastewater discharges, VOC emission thresholds, hazardous waste streams or land-use contaminant burdens associated with the AI API platform. Data-center and cloud-infrastructure providers hosting the inference workloads remain responsible for their own power, cooling, e-waste and environmental compliance.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Not Applicable. No Civil Defense fire permit, Fire and Emergency New Zealand operational certificate, or structural load inspection is required for a digital AI/LLM API platform because no factory, chemical plant, assembly line or warehouse exists. Any conventional office or home workspace, if occupied, must still comply with the Building Act 2004 means-of-escape requirements and the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 welfare obligations, but those are ordinary premises compliance duties rather than an industrial fire-safety license.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) of New Zealand; online portal: myIR Secure Online Services; corporate/entity registration via the New Zealand Companies Office and New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) Registry
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: For an NZ-incorporated limited company, first incorporate with the New Zealand Companies Office and obtain an NZBN. Then apply to Inland Revenue for an IRD number using the prescribed application for a non-resident-owned company, which requires the NZBN, registered office address in New Zealand, director and shareholder details, and the company's tax residency status. After the IRD number is issued, GST registration is completed through myIR using the GST registration application; the GST registration number is the same as the IRD number. For a foreign non-resident entity not carrying on an active business in New Zealand, an IRD number may still be required for GST registration when supplying remote services or imported goods to New Zealand; the application is made through myIR or using the relevant Inland Revenue form, and the entity must provide foreign registration evidence, jurisdictional tax identification, contact details, and estimated New Zealand turnover. No separate TIN/VAT ID is issued under a different numbering sequence because the IRD number operates as the unified tax identifier in New Zealand.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No US-style check-the-box election is available under New Zealand law. Eligible close-held resident companies may elect look-through company (LTC) treatment under the Income Tax Act 2007 to have income, expenses, gains, and losses attributed to shareholders; consolidated group treatment is available for groups of wholly owned New Zealand resident companies; tax loss grouping elections are permitted between commonly owned companies. Hybrid mismatch rules under the Taxation (Neutralising Base Erosion and Profit Shifting) Act 2018 apply and override elective outcomes that would otherwise exploit hybrid entity mismatches.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 (New Zealand)
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 of taxable supplies in any continuous 12-month period, including for non-resident offshore suppliers of remote services supplied to New Zealand GST-registered or non-registered recipients; registration is voluntary below this threshold but mandatory once the threshold is crossed.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: New Zealand does not operate a real-time fiscal clearance, continuous transaction control, or digital anti-fraud stamping regime. GST-registered suppliers must issue compliant GST tax invoices and file GST returns electronically through myIR on a monthly, two-monthly, or six-monthly filing cycle depending on turnover and registration preference. E-invoicing is voluntary and available through the Peppol network; Inland Revenue may access transactional records through electronic data capture or information requests, but there is no mandatory API clearance stamping requirement.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating is available under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985. For goods, supplies are zero-rated when they are exported by the supplier or delivered to a non-resident who exports them from New Zealand within the statutory timeframe. For services, including AI/LLM inference API subscriptions and token-based digital platform services, zero-rating applies when the services are supplied to a non-resident recipient who is outside New Zealand at the time of supply and when the services are not supplied for direct use or consumption in New Zealand; remote services supplied to an offshore GST-registered business may also be zero-rated if the supplier holds sufficient documentary evidence of the recipient's non-resident status and the absence of New Zealand use. Services supplied to New Zealand-resident customers remain subject to 15% GST.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: For tangible exports: New Zealand Customs Service Trade Single Window (TSW) export declaration or outward cargo report for departing goods
Commercial invoice and packing list identifying the New Zealand supplier, overseas buyer, and exact goods description
For sea: Bill of Lading; for air: Air Waybill evidencing physical export from New Zealand
GST tax invoice issued by the New Zealand supplier stating the zero-rating basis and the overseas customer's identity

Evidence of cross-border payment received in the New Zealand entity's bank account, such as bank SWIFT/credit advice or foreign exchange repatriation record, demonstrating settlement from the foreign customer
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue may audit zero-rated export supplies and retrospectively assess GST, plus use-of-money interest, if the exporter or service supplier cannot substantiate the non-resident status of the recipient, physical export of goods, or the fact that services were not consumed in New Zealand. Civil shortfall penalties apply on the resulting GST shortfall: 20% for lack of reasonable care or an unacceptable tax position, 40% for gross carelessness, 100% for an abusive tax position, and 150% for evasion; interest runs from the original due date of the output tax that would have applied had the supply not been zero-rated. New Zealand has no statutory foreign-exchange repatriation deadline; the 180-day figure is used as an evidentiary retention and audit review benchmark rather than as a legal repatriation requirement.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand operates a fully liberalised capital and current account convertibility framework. There are no foreign exchange controls, no central bank approval requirements for inward or outward capital flows, and no restrictions on the repatriation of profits, dividends, royalties, or capital. The New Zealand dollar is freely floating and trades actively in global markets. Resident and non-resident entities may hold foreign currency bank accounts domestically and abroad without prior authorisation. There are no surrender requirements for export proceeds, and businesses are not required to convert foreign currency receipts into NZD by any statutory timeline. The only relevant obligations flow from the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, which requires banks to conduct customer due diligence and report suspicious transactions. For a licensed AI/LLM API platform generating revenue from global customers, the convertibility of USD, EUR, or other settlement currencies into NZD for operational expenses and onward dividend distributions is entirely unrestricted. Profit remittance hurdles are effectively nil from a regulatory perspective, provided the underlying transactions are commercially genuine, fully documented, and consistent with the company's registered business purpose. Banks may still apply internal compliance screening to high-risk payment sources such as cryptocurrency-derived funds, but this is a KYC matter rather than a statutory exchange control barrier.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: New Zealand imposes no statutory surrender timeline and no mandatory conversion ratio for export foreign currency receipts. Exporters may retain all proceeds in foreign currency, hold them in offshore accounts, or convert them freely at commercial bank rates subject only to internal bank policy and AML/CFT record-keeping requirements.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Fintech electronic money institutions (EMIs) have limited viability for core treasury operations in New Zealand. The jurisdiction does not have an EU-style EMI licence regime, and non-bank digital wallet providers are not authorised to offer full corporate deposit-taking services. Offshore digital EMIs may provide payment initiation or card issuing services with limited adoption by local clearing systems, but they cannot replace a licensed New Zealand bank for capital escrow, foreign exchange settlement, or commercial trade finance. Legal constraints include the need for registration on the Financial Service Providers Register (FSPR) and compliance with the AML/CFT Act if operating locally. For the AI/LLM API platform, an EMI could be used solely as a supplementary collections gateway, but the primary treasury account must be held with an NZ-registered licensed bank to secure FMA/SOE oversight, clearing payment access, and credible audit trail.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: New Zealand banks generally require at least one director or a senior authorised signatory to complete a live identity verification process. Physical in-branch attendance is preferred for first-time corporate clients, particularly for a newly registered limited company with non-resident directors. Remote onboarding is possible through video identity verification and electronic execution, but most tier-1 banks mandate a commercial relationship review with the beneficial owners. Some banks accept consular certification or apostilled documents for directors who cannot travel, yet the final approval committee often insists on a recorded interview. For a fully remote offshore director, a professional intermediary with knowledge of the client, such as a New Zealand lawyer or accountant bound by AML obligations, may certify the KYC pack. Without a physical or video interview, onboarding viability drops materially across all tier-1 banks.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Beneficial ownership for a New Zealand limited company ultimately held by a discretionary trust in a low-tax jurisdiction.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified copy of the trust deed, an up-to-date register of beneficiaries issued by the trustee, a notarised statement of source of wealth from each settlor, and a New Zealand tax declaration confirming the company is tax-resident and that all distributions to the trust are disclosed to Inland Revenue.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Commercial revenue and capital inflows originating from cryptocurrency platforms or USDC-denominated treasury operations.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Independent wallet audit report with chain analysis showing source of crypto funds, exchange KYC/AML statements, a clear corporate resolution approving digital asset treasury policy, and signed customer agreements proving that crypto receipts map to actual AI/LLM API usage invoices.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident directors sharing addresses in high-risk or sanctioned-adjacent jurisdictions without any physically verifiable local footprint.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Apostilled passports, utility bills not older than 90 days, a New Zealand Companies Office director certificate, confirmation from a New Zealand chartered accountant acting as an authorised AML supervisor, and an irrevocable undertaking from the local accounting firm to maintain updated director identity evidence.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unusual cross-border payment routing with mismatch between invoicing jurisdiction and ultimate counterparty beneficial owner.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Audited trade ledger verifying API consumption by counterparty, signed service agreements with all material customers, bank statement from the originating financial institution confirming the remitter's identity, and a group structure presentation showing every entity between the platform and the settling bank.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound equity or shareholder loan capital for the NZ limited company must arrive via SWIFT MT103 from the originating shareholder's bank account using the company's Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) and NZ BIC. The remittance reference should include 'Shareholder Capital Subscription — NZ_LTD ISIC 6201' to prevent misclassification. Since New Zealand has no exchange control approval or mandatory FX declaration, the receiving bank will generate a post-verification certificate confirming settlement and credit of funds. The company should then issue shares or a registered loan agreement, and complete a capital verification memorandum signed by a New Zealand chartered accountant. For funding routed through a crypto or USDC intermediary, the bank will require a detailed crypto-to-fiat conversion flow and a source-of-funds trail before accepting the credit. Use of an underlying purpose code is optional, but if required, banks commonly reference 'capital payments' or 'investment in enterprise' under the IMF BPM6 classification. No lodgement of the investment is required under the Overseas Investment Act for the AI/LLM API sector, unless sensitive land or significant business assets thresholds are triggered.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: For outbound trade disbursements the company should maintain segregated clearing rails. Standard supplier and infrastructure payments are made through SWIFT MT103 messages using NZD, USD, or CNH accounts, with invoice reference numbers embedded in the payment details. Large capital expenditures for GPU cloud capacity or model inference hardware are best settled via commercial documentary letters of credit (L/C) when the counterparty requires proof of shipment; otherwise wire transfer with a clean shipping guarantee and bill of lading copy is viable. For recurring API licensing fees, a master service agreement plus monthly statement invoice is sufficient for direct SWIFT transfers. Companies may also use documentary collections (D/P at sight) for moderate-value import/export arrangements where neither full prepayment nor L/C is preferred. All outbound payments must be consistent with the company's registered business description; any remittance to a tax haven or to a non-invoiceable provider will trigger additional AML review and likely require negative media screening.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Domestic FX forward contracts (USD/NZD, EUR/NZD, CNY/NZD) with tenors up to 12 months and bank-approved underlying trade exposure
Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) on frontier-market currencies where local convertibility is constrained, restricted to verified trade payables or receivables
Cross-currency swaps for matched funding of USD venture-capital-style loans converted to NZD operating balances, subject to board-approved net open position limits
Vanilla FX options (call/put on NZD crosses) for downside protection on AI/LLM hardware imports and cloud infrastructure costs

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return under Section 244 of the Companies Act 1993, confirming registered office, address for service, director particulars, issued shares and constitution details
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Registrar of Companies, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 28 days after each anniversary of the date of incorporation; for example, a company incorporated on 15 May must file on or before 12 June every year
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: A late-filing fee of NZD 46.60 applies and the company is marked non-compliant; continued failure allows the Registrar to issue a notice of intention to remove the company under Section 318 of the Companies Act 1993, and if no objection is filed within the statutory notice period, the company is struck off, dissolved, and its property vests in the Crown

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual beneficial ownership statement and update of the beneficial ownership register for holders with a 25% or more direct or indirect interest or control
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Registrar of Companies, MBIE
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Filed together with the annual return no later than 28 days after the incorporation anniversary; reportable changes arising from share transfers or allotments must be notified within 30 working days of the change being registered in the company's member register
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to maintain or file the beneficial ownership statement is an offence under the Companies (Beneficial Ownership Disclosure) Amendment Act 2022, punishable by fines up to NZD 10,000 for the company and continuing per-day penalties for directors; the non-compliance may also be relied on in Registrar strike-off proceedings

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: General purpose financial statements and independent auditor's report, when the company is large or an FMC reporting entity under the Financial Reporting Act 2013
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Registrar of Companies, MBIE
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 20 working days after the board signs and dates the financial statements; for a 31 March balance date company this normally occurs in the following financial year
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file audited financial statements is an offence under the Financial Reporting Act 2013; directors and senior managers may face fines up to NZD 50,000 plus daily penalties for continued default, and the Registrar may use the default as a basis for removal of the company from the register

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual corporate income tax return (IR4) and payment of any terminal tax liability
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: For a standard 31 March balance date, the IR4 return is due by 7 July following the balance date and terminal tax is due by 7 April following the balance date; an approved tax-agent extension may extend the return-filing due date to 31 March of the following year
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: IRD imposes late-filing penalties, escalating daily penalties, and late-payment interest at the prescribed IRD rate on unpaid terminal tax; continued failure to file may lead to prosecution under the Tax Administration Act 1994 and personal liability of directors where tax has been deducted or collected but not remitted

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: A compulsory independent audit by a licensed certified auditor is legally required when a New Zealand company is 'large' under the Financial Reporting Act 2013, namely at each of the two most recent consecutive balance dates it meets any of the following quantitative triggers: (a) total assets exceed NZD 60 million; (b) total annual revenue exceeds NZD 30 million; or (c) it employs an average of 50 or more full-time equivalent employees. A financial-market conduct (FMC) reporting entity, an overseas company carrying on business in New Zealand, or a company whose constitution or shareholders validly require an audit is also subject to mandatory audit irrespective of these thresholds.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: New Zealand equivalents to International Financial Reporting Standards (NZ IFRS) for Tier 1 and large entities; NZ IFRS with Reduced Disclosure Regime (NZ IFRS RDR) for eligible Tier 2 entities; and NZ IFRS for Small and Medium-Sized Entities for qualifying smaller entities, all as issued by the External Reporting Board (XRB) under the Financial Reporting Act 2013. Statutory audits are performed by licensed auditors under XRB auditing and assurance standards.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: The annual return must contain a current beneficial ownership confirmation identifying each beneficial owner holding, directly or indirectly, 25% or more of the shares or voting rights or otherwise exercising significant control. The company must keep an internal beneficial ownership register and take reasonable steps to verify beneficial owners before filing. Share allotments must be notified to the Registrar within 20 working days; registered-office changes within 10 working days; director appointments and cessations within 20 working days; and a transfer of shares must be recorded in the Register of Members immediately upon registration. Where a transfer crosses or changes the 25% beneficial ownership threshold, the beneficial ownership register must be updated and the Companies Office notified within 30 working days of the transfer being registered, in addition to being confirmed in the next annual return.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Members (including all share transfers, allotments, and beneficial ownership information where required)
Register of Directors (including consents and full statutory particulars)
Register of Charges and Debentures (if any security interest or debt instrument exists)
Minute Book of Board and Shareholder Resolutions
Beneficial Ownership Register under the Companies (Beneficial Ownership Disclosure) Amendment Act 2022

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No federal R&D tax credit currently available for general AI software development beyond the 15% R&D Tax Credit (RDTI) for eligible R&D expenditure; no patent box regime; free-zone incentives not applicable as New Zealand operates a unitary national tax system. Losses may be carried forward indefinitely subject to continuity of ownership (49% or more) or business continuity tests, but for illustration the schema requires a numeric cap; New Zealand does not have a 5-year limit, so we set to 10 to reflect the practical continuity requirement, though statutorily indefinite.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 (Company Income Tax Return) filed via myIR (Inland Revenue's electronic filing portal)
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Generally 7 months after the company's balance date (e.g., for a 31 March balance date, the filing deadline is 7 July). If the company uses a tax agent with an extension, the deadline can be extended to the following 31 March or as notified by Inland Revenue.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total income (turnover, gross income, including all assessable income from AI API platform subscriptions and usage fees).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report worldwide income unless the company is a non-resident company with attributable income subject to special rules. For an NZ Ltd, report all income derived from global API sales. Do not deduct non-deductible expenses yet.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Expenses (total deductible expenditure, including R&D costs, cloud hosting, staff, marketing, and royalties paid to non-residents).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Only expenses incurred in deriving assessable income are deductible. Payments to non-residents (e.g., outbound royalties or interest) must be separately disclosed in Box 22 or Supplementary return if withholding tax applies. Transfer pricing adjustments must be factored in before claiming deductions.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net taxable income (Box 1 minus Box 2, adjusted for tax adjustments and add-backs).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the company is a controlled foreign company (CFC) shareholder or has foreign dividend or interest income, add deemed income. For non-resident-owned NZ Ltd, ensure any exempt foreign dividend or branch equivalent adjustments are properly excluded.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Loss carry forward claimed (offset prior-year tax losses).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A loss may be carried forward only if the company satisfies the shareholder continuity (49% or more) or business continuity (same business) tests. For an AI LLM API platform, any change in ownership or substantial new business line may invalidate the loss offset. Report exact amount.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax on taxable income (income tax at 28% for the 2024/25 and 2025/26 income years).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Calculate 28% of Box 3 (after loss offset). There is no lower corporate rate for AI companies. Any foreign tax credits (FTC) for non-resident withholding taxes on outbound or inbound cross-border payments are claimed here, limited to the New Zealand tax payable on that foreign income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Imputation credit account (ICA) and dividend information for non-resident shareholders.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the NZ Ltd pays dividends to non-resident shareholders, attach a separate dividend statement. For a wholly non-resident-owned company, the dividend may be subject to Non-Resident Withholding Tax (NRWT) or the Approved Issuer Levy (AIL) if the dividend is fully imputed. Report the imputation credits attached and ensure the rate of NRWT/AIL is correct. If the company has no imputation credits, NRWT at 30% applies unless reduced under a DTA.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty of NZ$250; late payment penalty of 1% of unpaid tax, increasing to 4% rate for sustained underpayment; periodic penalties of 1% per month for up to 6 months; and use-of-money interest (currently 9.98% for underpayments). Fraudulent evasion can lead to criminal prosecution under the Tax Administration Act 1994, with imprisonment up to 5 years and fines up to NZ$50,000 (plus triple tax shortfall penalties).

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: Non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) on dividends is 30%, but reduced to 5% if the dividend is fully imputed and an approved issuer levy (AIL) election is made. Without imputation, the 30% NRWT applies to gross dividends, subject to DTA reduction (commonly 15% for portfolio, 5% for substantive shareholding).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To claim a reduced DTA rate, the non-resident shareholder must provide: (1) a completed IR 419 certificate of residence for the relevant treaty jurisdiction, valid for the income payment year, and (2) evidence of beneficial ownership of the dividend (not a conduit). The NZ payer must obtain the certificate before the payment is made or within a reasonable time (typically before filing the return) to apply the reduced NRWT rate. If the reduced rate is not applied, a refund claim can be made through the IRD 'Email the refund for non-resident withholding tax' process, but the process is rigorous. For AIL, the company must be an approved issuer and pay AIL at 2% on fully imputed dividends, which replaces NRWT entirely.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Interest: NRWT is 15% (2% AIL may be available for interest paid to an approved issuer levy election, subject to anti-avoidance rules); treaty rates vary (typically 10% for interest). Royalties: NRWT is 15%; under most NZ DTAs, royalty withholding is 5% or 10%, but payments for software (including AI model licensing or API access fees) are generally treated as 'royalties' if they are for the right to use the intellectual property. For AI API platform revenue, characterisation as 'software as a service' vs 'royalty' is critical; pure API usage fees for customers are generally business profits, not royalties. Outbound royalties paid by the NZ entity to a non-resident parent or licensor attract NRWT at 15% unless a DTA reduces it (commonly 5%). Substantiation of beneficial ownership and residency is mandatory for relief.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: New Zealand does not have a distinct local currency threshold (NZD) for mandatory Local File / Master File preparation like OCDE countries. However, the tax administration requires transfer pricing documentation to be prepared and retained if the value of cross-border related-party transactions exceeds NZ$1 million for purchases or NZ$1 million for sales (and for loans, if the value of the loan exceeds NZ$5 million). In practice, any material related-party transaction must be documented on an arm's-length basis.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not have a formal separate Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) law like the UAE, but the CFC and general anti-avoidance rules (GAAR) require an NZ company to have real economic substance. Core Income-Generating Activities (CIGA) within the context of the OECD BEPS Actions 8-10 and a limited-risk entity analysis apply. For an AI LLM API platform, the company must demonstrate that it has the significant people functions (management, development, and risk control) in NZ to justify its profits and prevent profit shifting to or from related overseas entities. The Inland Revenue can recharacterize transactions under the GAAR (section BG 1, Income Tax Act 2007) if the economic substance of the arrangement is a tax avoidance scheme.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Intentionally omitting or understating revenue derived from AI API token sales, or knowingly claiming fictitious R&D deductions or inflated intercompany royalties to reduce taxable profit below the 28% corporate tax rate.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Tax Administration Act 1994, sections 143A and 143B: evasion shortfall penalty of 150% of the evaded tax; criminal conviction fines up to NZ$50,000 for individuals and NZ$100,000 for companies; imprisonment up to 5 years for directors or officers under section 143A(2)(g) and 146.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Under the Companies Act 1993 section 135, a director who allows trading while insolvent or engages in tax evasion may be personally liable for company debts. The court can order civil asset restitution under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009. Travel can be restricted through a customs departure ban under the Tax Administration Act 1994 section 157 if tax debt remains unpaid. Imprisonment is possible for up to 5 years.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Manipulation and Thin Capitalisation
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging a non-arm's-length mark-up for intra-group AI algorithm licences or using excessive intercompany debt to strip profits via interest deductions, and failing to prepare contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation when the cross-border related-party transaction threshold (NZ$1 million) is exceeded.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Income Tax Act 2007, sections GC 6 to GC 14 (transfer pricing adjustment) and section GC 15 (thin capitalisation) deny excess interest deductions, resulting in additional income tax of 28%, plus use-of-money interest, and shortfall penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994 (up to 40% for lack of reasonable care or 100% for abusive tax position).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly sign tax returns with false transfer pricing statements can be personally liable for penalties under section 148 of the Tax Administration Act 1994. Courts may pierce the corporate veil under the Companies Act 1993 if the company is an agent or sham, and directors can be barred from managing a company for up to 5 years under section 383.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using the NZ company as a shell without substantive operations, receiving API payments via cryptocurrency (USDC) and routing them through opaque corporate structures to obscure beneficial ownership, or failing to report cross-border currency movement of funds exceeding NZ$10,000 to the Financial Intelligence Unit.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT) imposes civil penalties up to NZ$200,000 for an individual and NZ$2 million for a body corporate for each violation of customer due diligence or record-keeping requirements, and criminal penalties for money laundering under the Crimes Act 1961 (sections 243-245) with imprisonment up to 7 years.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors are personally liable for AML/CFT compliance obligations if they knowingly allow the company to be used for money laundering or terrorist financing. Financial Markets Authority or reserve bank can issue a Pecuniary Penalty order against the director. Courts can order asset forfeiture and impose travel bans. Additionally, the OECD-based 'global transparency' regime under the Companies Act requires directorship details to be publicly available, so a director cannot rely on nominee secrecy.
